Weather for Readers: The Isobar Edit

The forecast you read at seven in the morning is a different document from the forecast that existed at six. Between those hours sits an editor, and in the case of the North Coast Bulletin, the editor is a retired ferry captain with strong opinions about the word “brisk”.

Meteorological offices publish probabilities. Readers want verdicts. The gap between the two is where weather writing lives, and the Bulletin has spent forty years refusing to close it from either side.

A typical edit: the model says “precipitation probability 60–80% after 1400”. The captain writes “rain by the school run; the kind that means it”. Accuracy, measured over four decades, is statistically indistinguishable. Reader trust is not.

The Bulletin's one concession to modernity is a heat map of reader complaints, which correlates almost perfectly with the use of the phrase “scattered showers”. Scattered where, the letters ask. Scattered why.

There is a lesson here for anyone who publishes machine output to human readers, and the captain will tell it to you for the price of a coffee: models forecast weather, but only sentences forecast a Tuesday.
